blanksInventory.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ is ______.
Large Counts: np ≥ ______ and n(1 − p) ≥ ______.

teacherQuestion.question: A poll of 1,000 adults and a poll of 4,000 adults both report p̂ = 0.52. How much smaller is the second poll’s standard deviation, and why isn’t it four times smaller?
look: n is under a square root in the SD formula
Uses the polls in the answer

pages.title: Bell ringer: statistics and sampling
pages.intro: About 10 minutes. Answer the four multiple-choice questions, then the free response.

questions.prompt: A survey of 80 randomly chosen seniors finds that 0.35 plan to take a gap year. What is 0.35?
choices: A margin of error for p
questions.why: 0.35 describes the 80 seniors who were sampled, so it is a statistic (p̂), not a parameter.
questions.hint: Does 0.35 describe the sample or every senior?

miss.why: A parameter describes the whole population. Nobody asked every senior.
p is the population value. This number came from 80 people.
A margin of error is a ± amount around an estimate, not the estimate itself.

questions.prompt: Which change makes the sampling distribution of p̂ less variable?
questions.why: The standard deviation of p̂ is √(p(1 − p)/n), so a larger n makes it smaller.
questions.hint: Which letter in the standard deviation formula can you change?

miss.why: Smaller samples bounce around more, not less.
The population size is not in the formula (as long as the sample is under 10% of it).
Volunteers add bias. They do not reduce variability.

questions.prompt: Samples of size n = 40 come from a population with p = 0.2. What is the mean of the sampling distribution of p̂?
questions.why: The sampling distribution of p̂ is centered at p, so its mean is 0.20.
questions.hint: Where is the sampling distribution of p̂ centered?

miss.why: 0.16 is p(1 − p), the piece inside the standard deviation.
8 is np, the expected count, not the expected proportion.
0.80 is 1 − p, the proportion of failures.

questions.prompt: For n = 40 and p = 0.2, is the Large Counts condition met?
questions.why: np = 40 × 0.2 = 8, which is less than 10, so the condition fails.
questions.hint: Find np and n(1 − p). Both need to be at least 10.

miss.why: The AP rule needs at least 10 expected successes, not 8.
n ≥ 30 is a rule of thumb for means, not for proportions.
n(1 − p) = 32, which is plenty. The problem is np.

frq.prompt: A school says that 60% of its students walk to school. A random sample of 50 students is taken.
parts: Describe the shape, center and variability of the sampling distribution of p̂.
Find the probability that p̂ is less than 0.50. Show your work.
guide: (a) Shape: approximately normal because np = 30 and n(1 − p) = 20 are both at least 10
frq.model: (a) Since np = 30 ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) = 20 ≥ 10, the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal, with mean 0.60 and standard deviation √(0.6 × 0.4 / 50) ≈ 0.069. (b) z = (0.50 − 0.60)/0.069 ≈ −1.44, so P(p̂ < 0.50) ≈ 0.075.
errors: Saying the shape is normal without checking Large Counts
Using p(1 − p)/n without the square root
Using 0.50 as the mean of the distribution
Describing the sample instead of the sampling distribution

pages.title: The candy jar contest
pages.story: Two classes are guessing the share of red candies in the same giant jar. Class A pulls 10 candies at a time; Class B pulls 100. Each class records many samples, and the class whose guesses land closest to the truth wins the jar.

widget.prompt: Before you simulate it: whose sample proportions will be more spread out?
widget.reveal: Class A’s proportions are much more spread out. Small samples bounce around; large samples stay close to the true proportion. The lab shows how much.

pages.title: Lab 1: Simulate the samples
pages.intro: Each run draws one random sample of size n from a jar where the true proportion of red is p, and records p̂.

widget.prompt: Set n and p, then run at least 30 samples. Then change n and watch the dot plot.

questions.prompt: As n went up, what happened to the spread of the p̂ values?
questions.why: Bigger samples average out more of the luck, so p̂ lands closer to p and the dot plot gets narrower.
questions.hint: Run 25 samples with n = 10, then 25 with n = 200. Compare the dot plots.

miss.why: Look again at the dot plot for n = 200 next to n = 10.
Wider would mean bigger samples are less reliable. Check the plot.

pages.title: Lab 2: Is a normal model OK?
pages.intro: The Large Counts condition: np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10.

widget.prompt: Sort each situation by whether the Large Counts condition is met.

cards.why: np = 15 and n(1 − p) = 35, both at least 10.
cards.miss: Find np and n(1 − p) first.

cards.why: np = 5, which is under 10, even though n is large.
cards.miss: A big n is not enough. Find np.

cards.why: np = n(1 − p) = 20, both at least 10.

cards.miss: Check the failures too: n(1 − p).

widget.hint: Compute both np and n(1 − p) for each card. Both have to be at least 10.
widget.why: The condition needs at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures.

pages.title: Lab 3: Hunt for the sample size

widget.prompt: With p = 0.5, find the sample size that makes the standard deviation of p̂ exactly 0.05.
widget.hint: Watch the readout. Quadrupling n halves the SD.
widget.wrong: Not yet. The readout has to say 0.050.

pages.title: The rule: the sampling distribution of p̂
sentences: The mean of the sampling distribution of p̂ equals {r-mean}.
Its standard deviation is the square root of p(1 − p) divided by {r-n}.
Use a normal model when np and n(1 − p) are both at least {r-ten}.

blanks.hint: Where was the dot plot centered in Lab 1?
blanks.why: p̂ is unbiased: its sampling distribution is centered at p.

miss.why: Only when p happens to be 0.5. In general it is centered at p.

blanks.hint: Which number did you change in Lab 3?
blanks.why: Dividing by n is why larger samples vary less.

miss.why: p is already in the top part, p(1 − p).

blanks.hint: Look at the intro of Lab 2.
blanks.why: At least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures.

miss.why: 30 is a rule of thumb for means, not proportions.
Some old books use 5. The AP course uses 10.

keyIdeas: p̂ is an unbiased estimator of p.
Larger samples give less variability: the SD shrinks with √n.
Check Large Counts before using a normal model.

pages.title: Check: score the contest
pages.intro: Time to judge the contest entries. A judge’s mistake comes first.

widget.prompt: Ana finds the standard deviation of p̂ for p = 0.3 and n = 84. Tap the step with the mistake.
steps: Check: np = 25.2 and n(1 − p) = 58.8, both at least 10.
So most p̂ values fall within about 0.005 of 0.3.

miss.0: Both counts are right and both are at least 10.
miss.1: The mean of p̂ is p. This step is right.
miss.3: This follows from the step before. Fix the earlier step first.

widget.hint: Compare Ana’s SD step with the rule card.
widget.why: Ana forgot the square root: √(0.21 / 84) = 0.05, not 0.0025.

questions.prompt: A population has p = 0.6. Samples of n = 150 are drawn. What is the standard deviation of p̂?

miss.why: 0.0016 is the variance. Take the square root.
That uses p/n inside the root instead of p(1 − p)/n.
That is √(p(1 − p)): you forgot to divide by n.

questions.prompt: Quadrupling the sample size does what to the standard deviation of p̂?
questions.why: n is under a square root, so 4 times the n divides the SD by √4 = 2.
questions.hint: Remember Lab 3: what happened between n = 25 and n = 100?

miss.why: n sits under a square root, so the SD shrinks by √4, not 4.
More data means less spread, not more.
n is in the formula, so the SD changes.

questions.prompt: Why is the sampling distribution of p̂ centered at p?
choices: p̂ is an unbiased estimator of p
Every sample has the same p̂
questions.why: On average over all random samples, p̂ equals p: it has no bias.
questions.hint: Think about the center of the dot plot in Lab 1.

miss.why: Even large samples miss p by a little. They are just close on average.
Your dot plot showed many different p̂ values.
A yes/no population is not normal. The center comes from no bias.

questions.prompt: Find the standard deviation of p̂ when p = 0.4 and n = 96.

miss.why: That is the variance. Take the square root.
That is p(1 − p). Divide by n and take the square root.

questions.prompt: Do larger random samples give more or less variability in p̂?
questions.hint: Look at your dot plots from Lab 1.
questions.why: Larger n means a smaller SD, so less variability.

miss.why: Your Lab 1 plot got narrower as n went up.

pages.title: Explain it, then your teacher’s question

questions.prompt: Explain why Class B’s samples of 100 give a more reliable estimate of the red share than Class A’s samples of 10. Use the idea of a sampling distribution.
questions.answer: The sampling distribution of p̂ for n = 100 has a smaller standard deviation than for n = 10, so Class B’s sample proportions cluster more tightly around the true proportion of red candies.
look: Refers to the sampling distribution of p̂
Says larger n gives a smaller SD
Ties it to the candy jar context

questions.prompt: A friend says, “If the sample is random, p̂ equals p.” Explain what is wrong, using the candy jar.
questions.answer: Random samples vary: one sample of 10 candies might have 20% red and another 40%, even though the jar is 30% red. p̂ equals p only on average over many samples.
look: Says p̂ varies from sample to sample
